tier_reason: Raised C to B: the README's plot (docs/hashbenches-skylake-clang.png) is backed by the peer-reviewed Software: Practice and Experience 2019 paper the README links, whose abstract (search snippets only; arXiv, lemire.me and r-libre blocked) reports beating optimized compiler code on Skylake and Ryzen, sometimes by more than 25%. The public harness lemire/constantdivisionbenchmarks hashbenches/time_hash_benches_clang.sh (clang -O3; lkk vs system vs slow) matches the plot, but the Clang version and exact CPU model are not on any page reachable here, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README text: 'In hashing benchmarks on Intel Skylake with Clang, this library outperforms compiler optimizations' and 'Faster than compiler-optimized divisions for known divisors'. Plot values read off the image (approximate, not printed as text): division instruction about 0.86 s at every divisor; compiler about 0.26-0.44 s; fastmod ('our approach (LKK)') about 0.25-0.30 s for most divisors. That is about 2.9-3.4x faster than the division instruction and up to about 1.7x faster than the compiler at the compiler's worst divisors (derived from plot reading). At the power-of-two divisors 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 both the compiler and LKK lines drop to about 0.02 s (no win there), and at divisors 5 and 6 the compiler line is slightly below LKK (about 0.27-0.28 s vs 0.30 s). Paper abstract (search snippet only): C implementations beat optimized code from state-of-the-art C compilers on Intel Skylake and AMD Ryzen, 'sometimes by more than 25%'.
corrections.workload: Latency-bound linear congruential generator ('hash benchmark'): seed = (seed*31 + 27961) % D repeated 100,000,000 times with D a compile-time constant from 2 to 64; whole-process time via bash 'time' for lkk (fastmod's LKK remainder), system (the compiler's x % D) and slow (x % d through a volatile divisor, i.e. the hardware division instruction). Harness: lemire/constantdivisionbenchmarks hashbenches (time_hash_benches_clang.sh); the script checks that all variants return the same exit code. The fastmod README shows the resulting plot for Clang on Skylake.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang -O3 (hashbenches/time_hash_benches_clang.sh in lemire/constantdivisionbenchmarks); Clang version not stated. fastmod's own Makefile builds its tests at -O3 but its 64-bit benchmarks (tests/modnbenchmark.cpp, tests/moddivnbenchmark.cpp) have no published results.
corrections.hardware: Intel Skylake (README; the harness script's host case is named 'skylake'); exact CPU model not stated on any page reachable here
corrections.caveats: The only quantitative evidence in the README is a plot image (values read by eye). The plot's harness is most likely lemire/constantdivisionbenchmarks/hashbenches (11 stars, research-only, not linked from the fastmod README): it times whole processes with bash 'time' on a single dependent LCG chain, so it measures latency of one remainder per iteration, not throughput. Clang version and exact CPU model are not stated on reachable pages. At power-of-two divisors the compiler is as fast as LKK, and at divisors 5 and 6 the compiler is slightly faster. The peer-reviewed paper (Lemire, Kaser, Kurz, Software: Practice and Experience 49(6), 2019, arXiv 1902.01961) could not be opened (arxiv.org, lemire.me, r-libre.teluq.ca blocked); its abstract via search snippets says the C code beats state-of-the-art compilers on Skylake and Ryzen 'sometimes by more than 25%', and the record's earlier snippet mentions 18 vs 72 cycles (unverified). Category is a weak fit: fastmod is 32-bit (and experimental 64-bit) integer remainder and division by a runtime-invariant divisor, not big-integer arithmetic. The 64-bit functions need __uint128_t and are not supported on Visual Studio.

notes: Tier raised C to B on the peer-reviewed SPE 2019 paper (abstract via search snippets only) plus a public research harness (lemire/constantdivisionbenchmarks hashbenches, clang -O3) that matches the README plot; A would need the paper's Clang version and CPU model. Shortcomings: plot-only evidence read by eye; no win at power-of-two divisors and slightly slower than compiler code at divisors 5 and 6; category big-integer-arbitrary-precision is a poor fit. License Apache-2.0, 352 stars, not a fork, not archived confirmed on github.com; last commit 2026-04-11 confirmed (commits atom feed), so active.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed Nature Computational Science 2022 paper (abstract via search snippet only: 122x and 34x faster than the reference and the fastest state-of-the-art implementations) matches the README speedup-factor column; the README table and public harness (src/benchmark.cpp, src/benchmark/cwtbench.py) name the MacBook Pro 2019 i9 but no compiler, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Calculating CWT 34-120x faster than all competitors' (C++ performance). Table (seconds, 10k-300 / 10k-3000 / 100k-300 / 100k-3000): fCWT C++ 0.005 / 0.04 / 0.03 / 0.32; CCWT (Python) 0.019 / 0.11 / 0.15 / 3.40; PyWavelets 0.10 / 1.17 / 1.06 / 12.69; Matlab 0.75 / 0.86 / 1.06 / 13.26; ssqueezepy 0.04 / 0.43 / 1.16 / 17.76; SciPy 0.19 / 1.82 / 2.11 / 18.70; Rwave (C) 0.18 / 1.84 / 2.28 / 23.22; Mathematica - / - / - / 27.83; Wavelib (C++) 0.25 / 2.55 / 4.85 / 45.04. README 'speedup factor' column (100k-3000): CCWT 10.63x, PyWavelets 34.29x, Matlab 35.85x, ssqueezepy 48.00x, SciPy 50.54x, Rwave 62.75x, Mathematica 75.20x, Wavelib 121.72x. All factors except CCWT's equal the competitor time divided by 0.37 s, not the table's 0.32 s (CCWT's uses 0.32 s) (derived from page data). The '34-120x than all competitors' headline is contradicted by the README's own CCWT row (10.63x) and shrinks at small sizes: at 10k-300 CCWT is 0.019 s vs 0.005 s (about 3.8x) and ssqueezepy 0.04 s (8x) (derived from page data). Paper abstract (search snippet only): 122 times and 34 times faster than the reference and the fastest state-of-the-art implementations. fCWT Python wrapper 0.66 s and Matlab wrapper 1.55 s at 100k-3000.
corrections.caveats: Evidence is the README table, which the README ties to the Nature Computational Science paper (Arts and van den Broek, 2022, cover article); the paper could not be opened (nature.com, doi.org and the PMC copy PMC10766549 blocked), and the abstract's 122x/34x was seen only in a search snippet. Harness asymmetries in src/benchmark.cpp: fCWT runs in single precision (float) with 8 threads and exhaustive FFTW plans, while the Rwave and Wavelib rows run double precision single-threaded (rwave::cwt and wavelib cwt take no thread count); the Python (cwtbench.py) and Matlab/Mathematica rows run through interpreters with default threading. benchmark.cpp hard-codes 300 frequencies (noct 6 x nvoi 50) and 5 runs, so the 3000-frequency C++ columns need source edits; cwtbench.py uses 3000 scales. src/benchmark/README.md reports different competitor times from the main table (MATLAB 18.28 s, Mathematica 38.86 s, PyWavelets 12.59 s, SciPy 19.56 s). The speedup factors use 0.37 s for fCWT (probably the paper's figure) while the table shows 0.32 s, and CCWT's 10.63x contradicts the '34-120x faster than all competitors' headline. The Matlab row (0.75 s at 10k-300 vs 0.86 s at 10k-3000) looks odd. No output equivalence check between implementations in the harness. Compiler not stated; CMakeLists.txt sets -fPIC -mavx -O2 on Unix with OpenMP. The default build links prebuilt FFTW (fftw3f) binaries bundled in libs/, which are GPL-2.0-or-later, hence usability mixed. Baselines are other CWT libraries, not an FFT incumbent; fCWT is a CWT built on FFTW, a weak fit for the fft category.

notes: Tier B confirmed on the peer-reviewed paper (abstract via search snippet only); README numbers match the record. Shortcomings: headline '34-120x than all competitors' contradicted by its own CCWT row (10.63x) and much smaller at 10k-300 (3.8x vs CCWT); 8-thread float fCWT vs single-thread double Rwave/Wavelib; speedup factors computed against 0.37 s not the table's 0.32 s; benchmark folder README gives different competitor times. Apache-2.0, 402 stars, 84 forks confirmed on github.com; last commit 2025-01-06 confirmed (commits atom feed), so stale.

tier_reason: Independent third-party run (hayguen/pffft_benchmarks, harness bench_pffft.c in hayguen/pffft) with gcc 9.3.0-17ubuntu1~20.04, Intel Core i7-8550U and CMAKEOPT empty (harness defaults) recorded in the platform's infos.txt; FFTW is the system libfftw3f whose version and build flags are not recorded, so B rather than A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc/g++ 9.3.0-17ubuntu1~20.04 (infos.txt in the platform directory); FFTW=ON and CMAKEOPT empty, so the bench/CMakeLists.txt defaults apply (Release, BENCH_ARCH native i.e. -march=native, BENCH_FAST_MATH ON) for the harness and the libraries it builds. FFTW is linked as the system-installed fftw3f (USE_BENCH_FFTW links fftw3f), whose version and build flags are not recorded. FFTW F(estim) uses FFTW_ESTIMATE; F(auto) uses FFTW_MEASURE only for N < 2400 and is left unmeasured (0) above that.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-8550U @ 1.80 GHz (4 cores, 8 threads, max 4.0 GHz), Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS x64 (infos.txt lscpu and /proc/cpuinfo)
corrections.caveats: Third-party harness from hayguen, maintainer of the PFFFT fork that competes with FFTW, but the result favours FFTW at most sizes. The result file does not state FFTW's version or build flags (system fftw3f package), so tier B rather than A; the run dates from 2020 and the harness at HEAD may differ from the one used. FFTW F(auto) is FFTW_MEASURE only for N < 2400 and is 0.000000 (not measured) for N >= 4096. FFTPACK is 1985 scalar code while FFTW uses SIMD codelets, so the gap is partly SIMD rather than algorithm. FFTW F(estim) is slower than FFTPACK for complex N >= 2^20 on this machine (5312 vs 4915 and 4952 vs 2511 MFLOPS), and PocketFFT and PFFFT beat FFTW F(estim) from complex N = 2^19 up and PFFFT beats it on most real sizes. FFTW's own benchFFT results (fftw.org/speed) and the Frigo and Johnson Proc. IEEE 2005 paper were not opened (fftw.org blocked in earlier runs; not retried). The GitHub repo is the generator repository and does not build without the OCaml-generated codelets; users should take release tarballs from fftw.org. GPL-2.0-or-later (copyleft). FFTW is a named incumbent baseline of the wave-8 fft category (FFTW, MKL FFT, KissFFT).

notes: Numbers match the i7-8550U result file exactly (complex N=64 7543 vs 34957/40030; N=1024 8579 vs 49570/55947; N=2^16 7382 vs 20507; real N=64 6193 vs 7555/11762, N=1024 8593 vs 18015/25766; reversals at complex 2^20 and 2^21). FFTW is the fft category's own named incumbent, so the boostorg/geometry, flame/blis and XNNPACK precedent (decision duplicate, folds into the known incumbent) likely applies; shortcomings if kept: FFTW version and build flags unrecorded, F(auto) unmeasured from 4096, slower than FFTPACK at complex 2^20-2^21. GPL-2.0 license, 3.1k stars and 721 forks confirmed on github.com; last commit 2026-06-10 confirmed (commits atom feed), so active; license is GPL-2.0-or-later per COPYRIGHT.
